concepts.title: Propositional logic and logical operators
concepts.summary: Not, and, or, implies, iff: the grammar of every mathematical statement.

blocks.title: Building statements from smaller ones
blocks.md:
**In this lesson you will learn to:**
- combine propositions with **not**, **and**, **or**, **implies** and **if and only if**
- work out the truth value of a compound statement with a truth table
- tell an implication apart from its converse and its contrapositive
- negate "and", "or" and "if… then" statements correctly

**You need:** lesson 1.1. A **proposition** is a sentence that is either true or false, and not both. You also met even and odd integers there.

## Why logic needs rules

Theorems are rarely single facts. They are built from small propositions glued together: "if $n$ is even **and** $n > 2$, **then** $n$ is not prime". To prove such a statement, or to say what its opposite is, you need to know exactly when the glued-together statement is true.

The glue words are called **logical connectives**. The key fact about them: the truth value of the compound statement depends **only** on the truth values of its parts, not on what the parts say.

So we use capital letters such as $P$ and $Q$ to stand for any propositions, and we write T for true and F for false.

A **truth table** lists every possible combination of truth values for the parts, one per row, and gives the truth value of the compound in each row. With one letter there are $2$ rows (T or F). With two letters there are $2 \times 2 = 4$ rows: TT, TF, FT, FF. Each new letter doubles the count, so $n$ letters give $2^n$ rows.

A truth table is a complete check. If two statements agree in every row, they agree in every possible situation.

## Not and and

**Negation.** $\neg P$ is read "not $P$". It is true exactly when $P$ is false, and false exactly when $P$ is true.

- $P$: "$7$ is prime" (T). $\neg P$: "$7$ is not prime" (F).
- $P$: "$2 < 5$" (T). $\neg P$ is "$2 \ge 5$" (F). **Careful:** $\neg P$ is **not** "$2 > 5$". The opposite of "less than" is "greater than **or equal to**". The negation must cover every case where $P$ fails, including $2 = 5$.

**Conjunction.** $P \land Q$ is read "$P$ and $Q$". It is true exactly when **both** parts are true.

$$\begin{array}{cc|c|c} P & Q & \neg P & P \land Q \\ \hline T & T & F & T \\ T & F & F & F \\ F & T & T & F \\ F & F & T & F \end{array}$$

- "$4$ is even and $4 > 3$": both parts true, so T.
- "$4$ is even and $4 > 7$": the second part is false, so the whole statement is F. One false part is enough to sink an "and".

In ordinary English, "but" often means $\land$: "$5$ is odd but $5$ is prime" is $P \land Q$.

blocks.question: Let $x = 3$. What is the negation of the proposition "$x > 1$"?
blocks.explanation: The negation must be true in **every** case where "$x > 1$" fails, including $x = 1$. So it is $x \le 1$. "$x < 1$" misses the case $x = 1$. "$x > -1$" and "$x \ne 3$" are unrelated statements, not opposites.

blocks.md:
## Or

**Disjunction.** $P \lor Q$ is read "$P$ or $Q$". It is true when **at least one** part is true. It is false only when both parts are false.

$$\begin{array}{cc|c} P & Q & P \lor Q \\ \hline T & T & T \\ T & F & T \\ F & T & T \\ F & F & F \end{array}$$

Notice the first row: when both parts are true, $P \lor Q$ is **true**. Mathematical "or" is **inclusive**: it means "one or the other or both".

- "$4$ is even or $4 > 3$": both true, so T.
- "$4$ is odd or $4 > 3$": the second part is true, so T.
- "$4$ is odd or $4 > 7$": both false, so F.

**Non-example.** On a menu, "soup or salad" usually means you may have one but not both. That is **exclusive** or. Mathematics never means this by "or". If a mathematician wants "exactly one", they say "exactly one" or "but not both".

This matters in proofs. If you know "$x = 0$ or $y = 0$" (for example from $xy = 0$), you must allow for both being $0$.

blocks.question: Let $P$ be "$6$ is even" and $Q$ be "$6$ is divisible by $3$". Both are true. What is the truth value of $P \lor Q$?
options: True, because at least one part is true
False, because "or" means only one of them can hold
It cannot be decided without more information
True only if we also know $P \land Q$ is false
blocks.explanation: Mathematical "or" is inclusive, so $P \lor Q$ is true whenever at least one part is true, including when both are. The second option describes exclusive or, which mathematics does not use. The truth values of $P$ and $Q$ are all we need, so nothing is undecided.

blocks.md:
## Implies

Almost every theorem has the shape "if $P$, then $Q$". This is the **implication** $P \Rightarrow Q$, read "$P$ implies $Q$". $P$ is the **hypothesis** and $Q$ the **conclusion**.

$P \Rightarrow Q$ is **false only when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false**. In every other row it is true.

$$\begin{array}{cc|c} P & Q & P \Rightarrow Q \\ \hline T & T & T \\ T & F & F \\ F & T & T \\ F & F & T \end{array}$$

Think of it as a promise: "If you score above $90$, I will give you a prize." The only way I break the promise is if you score above $90$ and get no prize. If you score below $90$, I have promised nothing, so whatever I do, I have not lied. That is why the last two rows are T.

**Examples with integers:**
- "If $4$ is even, then $4^2$ is even": T $\Rightarrow$ T, so true.
- "If $4$ is even, then $4 > 7$": T $\Rightarrow$ F, so false.
- "If $3$ is even, then $3 > 7$": F $\Rightarrow$ F, so **true**. An implication with a false hypothesis is called **vacuously true**.

**Other ways to say $P \Rightarrow Q$:** "$Q$ whenever $P$", "$P$ only if $Q$", "$P$ is sufficient for $Q$", "$Q$ is necessary for $P$". Note that "$P$ only if $Q$" is $P \Rightarrow Q$, not $Q \Rightarrow P$.

blocks.title: Two classic traps with implication
blocks.md:
1. **A false hypothesis makes the implication true.** "If $2 + 2 = 5$, then the moon is made of cheese" is a true implication. It says nothing about the moon, because the hypothesis never happens. You will use this in lesson 1.4 to show that the empty set is a subset of every set.
2. **An implication is not its converse.** "If $n = 4$ then $n$ is even" is true. Swapping the parts gives "if $n$ is even then $n = 4$", which is false ($n = 6$). Proving $Q \Rightarrow P$ does not prove $P \Rightarrow Q$.

blocks.prompt: Match each compound statement to exactly when it is true.

pairs.right: At least one of $P$, $Q$ is true
It is not the case that $P$ is true and $Q$ is false
$P$ and $Q$ have the same truth value

blocks.md:
## If and only if, and equivalence

**Biconditional.** $P \iff Q$, read "$P$ if and only if $Q$" (often shortened to "iff"), means $P \Rightarrow Q$ **and** $Q \Rightarrow P$. It is true exactly when $P$ and $Q$ have the **same** truth value: both T or both F.

- "$n$ is even $\iff$ $n + 1$ is odd" is true for every integer $n$.
- "$n = 4 \iff n$ is even" is false for $n = 6$: the right side is T, the left is F.

Definitions use "if" but really mean "iff": in lesson 1.1 you saw "$n$ is even $\iff n = 2k$ for some integer $k$".

**Logical equivalence.** Two compound statements are **logically equivalent**, written $\equiv$, if they have the same truth value in **every** row of the truth table. For example, $\neg(\neg P) \equiv P$: "it is not true that $7$ is not prime" says the same as "$7$ is prime". Equivalent statements can replace each other anywhere in a proof.

Two special kinds of formula:
- A **tautology** is true in every row. Example: $P \lor \neg P$ ("$n$ is even or $n$ is not even").
- A **contradiction** is false in every row. Example: $P \land \neg P$. Reaching one is the engine of proof by contradiction (lesson 1.9).

blocks.explanation:
$P \land 
eg P$ needs $P$ and $
eg P$ both true, which never happens. The other three are tautologies: $P \lor 
eg P$ always has one true part, and $P \Rightarrow P$ and $P \iff P$ can never have a true side paired with a false side.

blocks.md:
## Converse, contrapositive and negation

Start from an implication $P \Rightarrow Q$, such as "if $n$ is a multiple of $4$, then $n$ is even" (true).

- Its **converse** is $Q \Rightarrow P$: "if $n$ is even, then $n$ is a multiple of $4$". False ($n = 2$). The converse can have a different truth value.
- Its **contrapositive** is $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$: "if $n$ is not even, then $n$ is not a multiple of $4$". True. The contrapositive **always** has the same truth value as the original. You will check this with a truth table below, and use it as a proof method in lesson 1.10.

A useful rewrite: $P \Rightarrow Q \equiv \neg P \lor Q$. Both are false only in the row $P$ T, $Q$ F.

**Negating.** These rules tell you the opposite of a compound statement:

$$\neg(P \land Q) \equiv \neg P \lor \neg Q, \qquad \neg(P \lor Q) \equiv \neg P \land \neg Q.$$

These are **De Morgan's laws**: "not both" means "at least one fails", and "not either" means "both fail". Negating swaps $\land$ and $\lor$.

An implication fails only when the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails, so

$$\neg(P \Rightarrow Q) \equiv P \land \neg Q.$$

The negation of "if $n$ is even then $n^2 > 10$" is "$n$ is even **and** $n^2 \le 10$" (for instance $n = 2$). The negation of an implication is an "and", never another "if… then".

blocks.question: Let $x$ be a real number. What is the negation of "if $x > 2$ then $x^2 > 4$"?
blocks.explanation:
Using $

eg Q$: the implication fails exactly when $x > 2$ holds and $x^2 > 4$ fails. The first two options are still implications, and the second is the **inverse**, which is not even equivalent to the negation. The third is $
eg P \lor Q$, which is equivalent to the original statement, not its negation.

blocks.question: A friend has proved "if a number is a multiple of $6$, then it is even". They now claim this also proves "every even number is a multiple of $6$". What is wrong?
options: Nothing: an implication and its converse are equivalent
They have used the converse, which need not have the same truth value; $4$ is even but not a multiple of $6$
They should have used the negation instead
The original statement is vacuously true, so it proves nothing
blocks.explanation: "Every even number is a multiple of $6$" is the converse $Q \Rightarrow P$, and $4$ shows it is false. Only the contrapositive ("not even implies not a multiple of $6$") comes for free. The negation would be a different statement, and the original is not vacuous: it has true hypotheses such as $12$.

blocks.title: Checking that an implication equals its contrapositive

steps.title: List every row
steps.md: $P$ and $Q$ are two letters, so there are $2^2 = 4$ rows: TT, TF, FT, FF. Checking all four covers every possible situation.

steps.title: Work out the helper columns
steps.md:
Before evaluating $
eg Q \Rightarrow 
eg P$, fill in $
eg Q$ and $
eg P$ by flipping each value. Doing this first avoids mistakes.

$$ egin{array}{cc|cc} P & Q & 
eg Q & 
eg P \ \hline T & T & F & F \ T & F & T & F \ F & T & F & T \ F & F & T & T \end{array}$$

steps.title: Evaluate both implications
steps.md:
Use the rule: an implication is false only when its hypothesis is T and its conclusion is F.

$$ egin{array}{cc|c|c} P & Q & P \Rightarrow Q & 
eg Q \Rightarrow 
eg P \ \hline T & T & T & T \ T & F & F & F \ F & T & T & T \ F & F & T & T \end{array}$$

For $
eg Q \Rightarrow 
eg P$ the hypothesis is $
eg Q$. It is F in rows 1 and 3, so those rows are vacuously T.

steps.title: Compare the columns
steps.md:
The two columns agree in all four rows, so $P \Rightarrow Q \equiv \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$. $\blacksquare$

The converse $Q \Rightarrow P$ fails this test: in row 3 ($P$ F, $Q$ T) it is F while $P \Rightarrow Q$ is T.

blocks.question: In the table above, why is $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$ true in row 3, where $P$ is F and $Q$ is T?
options: Because its hypothesis $\neg Q$ is false, so the implication is vacuously true
Because $P \Rightarrow Q$ is true in that row
blocks.explanation: In row 3, $\neg Q$ is F, and any implication with a false hypothesis is true. (Here $\neg P$ also happens to be T, but in row 1 both are F and the implication is still T for the same vacuous reason.) Using the value of $P \Rightarrow Q$ would assume what we are trying to show.

blocks.prompt: Put these steps in order to negate "if $n$ is even, then $n^2$ is divisible by $4$".
items: Identify the parts: $P$ is "$n$ is even" and $Q$ is "$n^2$ is divisible by $4$".
Recall that $P \Rightarrow Q$ fails only when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false.
Write it in words: "$n$ is even and $n^2$ is not divisible by $4$".

blocks.title: Your turn: De Morgan's law by truth table
blocks.problem:
Use a truth table to show that $
eg(P \lor Q) \equiv 
eg P \land 
eg Q$. Then use it to negate "$x < 0$ or $x > 5$" for a real number $x$.
blocks.solution:
**Truth table.** Fill in $P \lor Q$, then its negation, then $
eg P$, $
eg Q$ and their conjunction.

$$ egin{array}{cc|c|c|cc|c} P & Q & P \lor Q & 
eg(P \lor Q) & 
eg P & 
eg Q & 
eg P \land 
eg Q \ \hline T & T & T & F & F & F & F \ T & F & T & F & F & T & F \ F & T & T & F & T & F & F \ F & F & F & T & T & T & T \end{array}$$

The columns for $
eg(P \lor Q)$ and $
eg P \land 
eg Q$ agree in all four rows, so the two are logically equivalent. $ lacksquare$

**Negating.** The negation of "$x < 0$ or $x > 5$" is "$x \ge 0$ **and** $x \le 5$", that is, $0 \le x \le 5$.

**Check your version:** did you list all four rows? Did your negation switch "or" to "and"? Did you negate $<$ as $\ge$ (not $>$)?

items.q: Why should "if $3$ is even then $3 > 7$" count as true? It feels wrong.
items.a: Think about "for every integer $n$, if $n$ is a multiple of $4$ then $n$ is even". We want this to be true. For $n = 3$ it reads "if $3$ is a multiple of $4$ then $3$ is even": F $\Rightarrow$ F. If that row counted as false, this true theorem would become false. Vacuous truth keeps general theorems working.
No. It only says that the row "$P$ true, $Q$ false" does not happen. "If $2 + 2 = 4$ then $7$ is prime" is true even though one fact has nothing to do with the other.

items.q: Is the negation of "$x > 2$" the statement "$x < 2$"?
items.a: No, it is $x \le 2$. The negation must be true whenever the original is false, and $x = 2$ makes "$x > 2$" false.

items.q: What is the difference between $\Rightarrow$ and $\iff$ in a definition?
items.a: Strictly, a definition is an "iff": $n$ is even exactly when $n = 2k$ for some integer $k$. Books often write "if" in definitions, but they always mean both directions.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.md:
- $
eg P$, $P \land Q$, $P \lor Q$ depend only on the truth values of $P$ and $Q$; a truth table with $2^n$ rows checks every case.
- Mathematical **or** is inclusive: it allows both.
- $P \Rightarrow Q$ is false **only** when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false; a false hypothesis makes it vacuously true.
- The **contrapositive** $
eg Q \Rightarrow 
eg P$ is equivalent to $P \Rightarrow Q$; the **converse** $Q \Rightarrow P$ is not.
- Negations: $
eg(P \land Q) \equiv 
eg P \lor 
eg Q$, $
eg(P \lor Q) \equiv 
eg P \land 
eg Q$, and $
eg(P \Rightarrow Q) \equiv P \land 
eg Q$.

questions.prompt: If $P$ is false and $Q$ is true, what is the truth value of $P \Rightarrow Q$?
options: It depends on what $P$ and $Q$ say
questions.explanation: An implication is false only when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false. With a false hypothesis it is (vacuously) true. Truth values alone decide it, so nothing else is needed.

questions.prompt: $P \Rightarrow Q$ is logically equivalent to its converse $Q \Rightarrow P$.
questions.explanation: When $P$ is false and $Q$ is true, $P \Rightarrow Q$ is true but $Q \Rightarrow P$ is false. It is the contrapositive $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$ that is equivalent.

questions.prompt: Which of these are logically equivalent to $P \Rightarrow Q$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation:
The contrapositive, $
eg P \lor Q$, and $
eg(P \land 
eg Q)$ (which equals $
eg P \lor Q$ by De Morgan) are all false only when $P$ is true and $Q$ false. The converse fails when $P$ is false and $Q$ true; $P \land Q$ is false whenever $P$ is false, while $P \Rightarrow Q$ is then true.

questions.prompt: Which statement is logically equivalent to $\neg(P \land Q)$?
questions.explanation:
By De Morgan's law, "not both" means "at least one fails": $
eg P \lor 
eg Q$. The first option says both fail, which is too strong: it is false when $P$ is T and $Q$ is F, yet $
eg(P \land Q)$ is then true.

questions.prompt: How many rows does a full truth table for a formula in three propositional variables $P, Q, R$ have?
questions.explanation: Each variable is true or false independently, giving $2^3 = 8$ assignments.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a tautology?
questions.explanation:
$P \lor 
eg P$ is true whichever value $P$ has. $P \land 
eg P$ is always false; $P \Rightarrow 
eg P$ is false when $P$ is true; $(P \Rightarrow Q) \Rightarrow P$ is false when $P$ is false (then $P \Rightarrow Q$ is true, and true $\Rightarrow$ false is false).

questions.prompt: $P \iff Q$ is true exactly when $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth value.
questions.explanation: $P \iff Q$ means $(P \Rightarrow Q) \land (Q \Rightarrow P)$, which holds when both are true or both are false.

questions.prompt: The negation of "$2 < 5$" is "$2 > 5$".
questions.explanation: The negation is "$2 \ge 5$". It must be true in every case where "$2 < 5$" would fail, and that includes equality.

questions.prompt: Which of these propositions are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: An "or" needs one true part, and $2 < 3$ is true. $(1 = 2) \Rightarrow (5 < 0)$ has a false hypothesis, so it is vacuously true. The "and" fails because $3 < 2$ is false; $(1 = 1) \Rightarrow (5 < 0)$ is T $\Rightarrow$ F, so false; and $\neg(2 < 3)$ is false because $2 < 3$ is true.

questions.prompt: Let $n$ be an integer. What is the contrapositive of "if $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even"?
options: If $n$ is even, then $n^2$ is even.
If $n$ is odd, then $n^2$ is odd.
If $n^2$ is odd, then $n$ is odd.
questions.explanation:
The contrapositive of $P \Rightarrow Q$ is $
eg Q \Rightarrow 
eg P$. Here $
eg Q$ is "$n$ is odd" and $
eg P$ is "$n^2$ is odd". The first option is the converse, the third is the inverse $
eg P \Rightarrow 
eg Q$, and the fourth is the negation.

questions.prompt: Suppose you know that $P \Rightarrow Q$ is false. How many of the two propositions $P$, $Q$ are true?
questions.explanation: An implication is false in exactly one row: $P$ true and $Q$ false. So exactly one of them is true.

questions.prompt: "$P$ only if $Q$" means the same as $P \Rightarrow Q$.
questions.explanation: "$P$ only if $Q$" says $P$ cannot happen without $Q$: whenever $P$ holds, $Q$ holds. That is $P \Rightarrow Q$. A common mistake is to read it as the converse $Q \Rightarrow P$.

questions.prompt: Let $n$ be an integer. What is the negation of "$n$ is even and $n > 2$"?
questions.explanation:
De Morgan: $
eg(P \land Q) \equiv 
eg P \lor 
eg Q$. For an integer, "not even" is "odd", and the negation of $n > 2$ is $n \le 2$. The first option forgets to swap "and" for "or"; the third negates $>$ as $<$ and misses $n = 2$; the fourth forgets to negate "$n$ is even".

concepts.title: Quantifiers: For all (∀) and There exists (∃)
concepts.summary: How $\forall$ and $\exists$ work, why their order matters, and how to negate them.

blocks.title: For every and there exists
blocks.md:
**In this lesson you will learn to:**
- read and write statements with $\forall$ ("for all") and $\exists$ ("there exists")
- prove and disprove each kind of statement
- negate quantified statements correctly
- see why the **order** of quantifiers changes the meaning

**You need:** lesson 1.1 (propositions and open sentences) and lesson 1.2 (not, and, or, implies, and how to negate them).

## From open sentences to propositions

In lesson 1.1 you met **open sentences** such as "$x^2 \ge 0$": their truth depends on a variable. Mathematics is full of claims about **every** number or **some** number, and the definitions in real analysis (bounded, limit, continuous) are long chains of "for every" and "there exists". You cannot read them without the language in this lesson.

We write an open sentence as $P(x)$, called a **predicate**. The variable takes values from a stated collection called the **domain**. Common domains:

- $\mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$, the **natural numbers**. (Some books include $0$; this course does not.)
- $\mathbb{Z}$, the integers, from lesson 1.1.
- $\mathbb{R}$, the **real numbers**: every point on the number line, such as $-2$, $0$, $\tfrac12$, $\sqrt{2}$ and $\pi$.

As in lesson 1.1, $x \in \mathbb{R}$ is read "$x$ is in $\mathbb{R}$", that is, "$x$ is a real number". Lesson 1.4 treats such collections (sets) properly.

The **domain matters**. "There is a number less than $1$" is true in $\mathbb{Z}$ (take $0$) but false in $\mathbb{N}$, where $1$ is the smallest number. Always say which domain you mean.

## For all: $\forall$

The **universal quantifier** $\forall$ is read "for all" or "for every".

$$\forall x \in A,\ P(x)$$

means "$P(x)$ is true for **every** $x$ in $A$". It is a single proposition: true or false.

- $\forall x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 \ge 0$. True: every real square is at least $0$.
- $\forall n \in \mathbb{N},\ n \ge 1$. True: $1$ is the smallest natural number.
- $\forall x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 > 0$. **False**, because of one edge case: $x = 0$ gives $0^2 = 0$, which is not $> 0$.

You can also restrict the variable: $\forall x > 0,\ P(x)$ means "for every real $x$ with $x > 0$, $P(x)$".

**How to prove it.** Let $x$ be an **arbitrary** element of $A$ (you may not choose it), then show $P(x)$. Your argument must work for every $x$ at once, just like the proofs with arbitrary even integers in lesson 1.1.

**How to disprove it.** Find **one** $x$ in $A$ where $P(x)$ is false: a counterexample. Above, $x = 0$ disproves "$\forall x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 > 0$".

blocks.question: Which value is a counterexample to $\forall x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 \ge x$?
blocks.explanation: $\left(\tfrac12\right)^2 = \tfrac14$, and $\tfrac14 < \tfrac12$, so the claim fails at $x = \tfrac12$. For $x = 2$: $4 \ge 2$. For $x = -1$: $1 \ge -1$. For $x = 0$: $0 \ge 0$ holds, since $\ge$ allows equality. A counterexample must make the statement **false**.

blocks.md:
## There exists: $\exists$

The **existential quantifier** $\exists$ is read "there exists" or "there is".

$$\exists x \in A,\ P(x)$$

means "$P(x)$ is true for **at least one** $x$ in $A$".

- $\exists x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 = 2$. True: $x = \sqrt{2}$ works (so does $-\sqrt{2}$; one is enough).
- $\exists n \in \mathbb{Z},\ n < 1$. True: $n = 0$.
- $\exists n \in \mathbb{N},\ n < 1$. **False**: same sentence, different domain.

**How to prove it.** Name one specific element, called a **witness**, and check that it works. No general argument is needed.

**How to disprove it.** Show $P(x)$ fails for **every** $x$ in $A$. One failure is not enough: "$\exists x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 = 2$" is not disproved by $x = 1$.

**Exactly one.** We write $\exists!\, x \in A,\ P(x)$ for "there is **exactly one** $x$ in $A$ with $P(x)$". To prove it you show two things: some $x$ works, and any two that work are equal.

- $\exists!\, x \in \mathbb{R},\ x + 3 = 5$. True: $x = 2$, and no other value works.
- **Non-example:** $\exists!\, x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 = 4$ is **false**, because both $2$ and $-2$ work. "At least one" is true here, "exactly one" is not.

blocks.prompt: Match each statement to the reason for its truth value.

pairs.right: False: every natural number is at least $1$

blocks.md:
## Negating quantifiers

To disprove a statement you prove its negation, so you must be able to write negations correctly.

"Not every $x$ has property $P$" means "some $x$ fails $P$". And "no $x$ has property $P$" means "every $x$ fails $P$". In symbols:

$$\neg\big(\forall x \in A,\ P(x)\big) \equiv \exists x \in A,\ \neg P(x)$$

$$\neg\big(\exists x \in A,\ P(x)\big) \equiv \forall x \in A,\ \neg P(x)$$

So negation **swaps** $\forall$ and $\exists$ and **negates** the predicate. Both changes are needed. (This mirrors De Morgan's laws from lesson 1.2: "for all" is a giant "and", "there exists" a giant "or".)

**Examples:**
- $\neg(\forall x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 \ge 0)$ is $\exists x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 < 0$.
- $\neg(\exists n \in \mathbb{N},\ n < 1)$ is $\forall n \in \mathbb{N},\ n \ge 1$.
- "Every student passed" negates to "some student did **not** pass", not "every student failed".

**Edge case: restrictions stay put.** The negation of $\forall x > 0,\ x^2 > x$ is $\exists x > 0,\ x^2 \le x$. The condition $x > 0$ only says which $x$ we are talking about, so it is **not** negated. (The negation is true: $x = \tfrac12$.)

blocks.title: Half a negation is a wrong negation
blocks.md:
The negation of "$\forall x,\ x > 0$" is "$\exists x,\ x \le 0$". Two tempting mistakes:

- "$\forall x,\ x \le 0$" negates only the predicate. It claims far too much.
- "$\exists x,\ x > 0$" swaps only the quantifier. It can be true at the same time as the original.

A correct negation is always true exactly when the original is false.

blocks.question: What is the negation of $\forall x > 0,\ x^2 > x$?
blocks.explanation: Swap $\forall$ for $\exists$, keep the restriction $x > 0$, and negate $x^2 > x$ to $x^2 \le x$. The first option forgets to swap the quantifier, the second wrongly negates the restriction, and the fourth forgets to negate the predicate.

blocks.md:
## The order of quantifiers matters

Many statements use more than one quantifier. Read them **left to right**: each choice is made knowing the ones before it.

$$\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\ \exists y \in \mathbb{R}:\ y > x \qquad \text{(true)}$$

"Give me any $x$; I can find a $y$ bigger than it." Since $y$ is chosen **after** $x$, it may **depend** on $x$: take $y = x + 1$.

$$\exists y \in \mathbb{R}\ \forall x \in \mathbb{R}:\ y > x \qquad \text{(false)}$$

"There is one $y$ bigger than every real number." Now $y$ is chosen **first** and must work for every $x$ at once, including $x = y$. No such $y$ exists.

An everyday version: "every person has a mother" ($\forall$ person $\exists$ mother) is true; "there is one woman who is everyone's mother" ($\exists$ mother $\forall$ person) is false.

In general, "$\exists y\ \forall x$" implies "$\forall x\ \exists y$" (one $y$ that works for all $x$ certainly works for each $x$), but not the other way round.

Two quantifiers of the **same** kind can be swapped: $\forall x\ \forall y$ means the same as $\forall y\ \forall x$, and likewise for $\exists\ \exists$.

To negate a chain, swap **every** quantifier, keep their order, and negate the predicate at the end:

$$\neg\big(\forall x\ \exists y:\ y > x\big) \equiv \exists x\ \forall y:\ y \le x.$$

blocks.question: Take $\mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$. Which statement is true?
blocks.explanation: $m = 1$ satisfies $1 \le n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. The first fails at $n = 1$ (no natural number is less than $1$); the second claims a largest natural number; the last fails for $m = 2$, $n = 1$.

cards.back:
"For **every** $x$ in $A$, $P(x)$." Prove with an arbitrary $x$; disprove with one counterexample.

*Example:* $\forall x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 \ge 0$.

"For **at least one** $x$ in $A$, $P(x)$." Prove with one witness.

*Example:* $\exists x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 = 2$ (witness $\sqrt{2}$).

There is **exactly one** $x$ in $A$ with $P(x)$.

*Example:* $\exists!\, x \in \mathbb{R},\ x + 3 = 5$. *Non-example:* $x^2 = 4$ (two solutions).

The collection the variable ranges over. Changing it can change the truth value.

*Example:* $\exists n,\ n < 1$ is true in $\mathbb{Z}$, false in $\mathbb{N}$.

A **specific** element that makes an $\exists$ statement true.

*Example:* $n = 0$ is a witness for $\exists n \in \mathbb{Z},\ n < 1$.

**Swap** $\forall \leftrightarrow \exists$ and negate the predicate; restrictions stay.

*Example:* $\neg(\forall x > 0,\ x^2 > x)$ is $\exists x > 0,\ x^2 \le x$.

In $\forall x\ \exists y$, $y$ **may depend on** $x$. In $\exists y\ \forall x$, one $y$ must work for all $x$.

*Example:* $\forall x\ \exists y:\ y > x$ is true; the swap is false.

blocks.question: A classmate wants to prove $\exists x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^3 = 8$. They start: "Let $x$ be an arbitrary real number." What should they do instead?
options: Carry on; arbitrary $x$ is always the right start
Give a witness: $x = 2$ is real and $2^3 = 8$
Check many values of $x$ and show most of them work
blocks.explanation: An $\exists$ statement needs one witness, nothing more. "Let $x$ be arbitrary" is how you start a $\forall$ proof, and here it is false that every $x$ works. Checking many values is unnecessary, and proving the negation would show the statement is **false**.

blocks.md:
## A definition from analysis: bounded functions

Here is a quantifier chain you will meet again in Level 2. Two pieces of notation:

- $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ means $f$ is a **function** that gives a real number $f(x)$ for every real $x$, such as $f(x) = x^2$. Functions are studied in lesson 1.6.
- $|t|$ is the **absolute value** of $t$: its distance from $0$, so $|3| = 3$ and $|-3| = 3$. Lesson 2.5 treats it in detail.

$f$ is **bounded** if some number $M$ caps the size of every value:

$$\exists M > 0\ \forall x \in \mathbb{R}:\ |f(x)| \le M.$$

- $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}$ is bounded: take $M = 1$, since $1 + x^2 \ge 1$.
- $f(x) = x$ is **not** bounded: whatever $M$ you choose, $x = M + 1$ has $|f(x)| > M$.

Notice the order: $M$ comes first, so one $M$ must work for **every** $x$. For $f(x) = x$, each single $x$ has some $M$ above it, but that is the weaker statement $\forall x\ \exists M$, which every function satisfies.

Next you will negate this definition step by step.

steps.title: Write the statement
steps.md:
A function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is **bounded** if

$$\exists M > 0\ \forall x \in \mathbb{R}:\ |f(x)| \le M.$$

We want the condition for $f$ to be **unbounded**: its negation.

steps.title: Negate the outer quantifier
steps.md: $\neg(\exists M > 0 \dots)$ becomes $\forall M > 0,\ \neg(\forall x \in \mathbb{R}:\ |f(x)| \le M)$. The restriction $M > 0$ stays as it is.

steps.title: Negate the inner quantifier
steps.md: $\neg(\forall x \dots)$ becomes $\exists x \in \mathbb{R},\ \neg(|f(x)| \le M)$. Work from the outside in, one quantifier at a time.

steps.title: Negate the predicate
steps.md:
$\neg(|f(x)| \le M)$ is $|f(x)| > M$. So $f$ is **unbounded** when

$$\forall M > 0\ \exists x \in \mathbb{R}:\ |f(x)| > M.$$

In words: no matter how big a cap $M$ you try, some value of $f$ breaks through it.

steps.title: Sanity check
steps.md: For $f(x) = x$: given any $M > 0$, the point $x = M + 1$ satisfies $|f(x)| = M + 1 > M$. Notice that $x$ depends on $M$, which is allowed because $\exists x$ comes after $\forall M$. So $f(x) = x$ is unbounded, as expected.

blocks.question: In the last step, why is $\neg(|f(x)| \le M)$ written as $|f(x)| > M$ and not $|f(x)| < M$?
options: Because negation reverses an inequality and also removes the equality
Because "not at most $M$" means "more than $M$"; $|f(x)| < M$ would still satisfy $|f(x)| \le M$
blocks.explanation: The negation must hold exactly when $|f(x)| \le M$ fails, which is when $|f(x)| > M$. Every value with $|f(x)| < M$ also has $|f(x)| \le M$, so it is not a negation at all. The sign of $M$ plays no part.

blocks.prompt: Put these steps in order to negate "$\forall M > 0\ \exists n \in \mathbb{N}:\ n > M$" (every positive number is beaten by some natural number).

blocks.title: Your turn: same words, different order
blocks.problem:
Decide which statement is true, and prove both answers.

(a) $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\ \exists y \in \mathbb{R}:\ x < y$.

(b) $\exists y \in \mathbb{R}\ \forall x \in \mathbb{R}:\ x < y$.

Hint: to show (b) is false, write its negation and prove that.
blocks.solution:
**(a) is true.** Let $x \in \mathbb{R}$ be arbitrary. Choose $y = x + 1$. Then $y \in \mathbb{R}$ and $x < x + 1 = y$. Since $x$ was arbitrary, (a) holds.

**(b) is false.** Its negation is $\forall y \in \mathbb{R}\ \exists x \in \mathbb{R}:\ x \ge y$. Let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ be arbitrary and choose $x = y$. Then $x \ge y$. So the negation is true, and (b) is false. $\blacksquare$

The pattern for a "$\forall\ \exists$" statement: let the universal variable be arbitrary, then **construct** the existential one, which may depend on it.

**Check your version:** in (a), did your $y$ depend on $x$ (it should)? In (b), did you swap both quantifiers and turn $<$ into $\ge$, not $>$?

items.q: If I find one example that works, have I proved a "for all" statement?
items.a: No. One example proves an $\exists$ statement. For $\forall$ you need an argument with an arbitrary element. But one example that **fails** does disprove a $\forall$ statement.

items.q: Can I just drop a quantifier when writing a proof?
items.a: Only if the meaning is still clear. "$x^2 \ge 0$" on its own is an open sentence. Writing "for every real $x$, $x^2 \ge 0$" makes it a proposition. Hidden quantifiers are the main cause of wrong negations.

items.q: What does $\forall x \in A,\ P(x)$ mean if $A$ has no elements?
items.a: It is true, vacuously. It says "if $x$ is in $A$ then $P(x)$", and the hypothesis never holds (lesson 1.2). Meanwhile $\exists x \in A,\ P(x)$ is false, because there is no witness.
No, it means **at least one**. $\exists x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 = 4$ is true even though two values work. Use $\exists!$ when you mean exactly one.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.md:
- $\forall x \in A,\ P(x)$: every $x$ works. Prove with an **arbitrary** $x$; disprove with **one counterexample**.
- $\exists x \in A,\ P(x)$: at least one $x$ works. Prove with **one witness**; $\exists!$ means exactly one.
- The domain is part of the statement: $\exists n,\ n < 1$ is true in $\mathbb{Z}$, false in $\mathbb{N}$.
- Negation swaps $\forall \leftrightarrow \exists$ and negates the predicate; restrictions like $x > 0$ stay.
- Order matters: in $\forall x\ \exists y$, $y$ may depend on $x$; in $\exists y\ \forall x$, one $y$ must serve every $x$.

questions.prompt: What is the negation of $\forall x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 \ge 0$?
questions.explanation: Negation turns $\forall$ into $\exists$ and negates the predicate: $\neg(x^2 \ge 0)$ is $x^2 < 0$. The first and fourth keep $\forall$; the third forgets to negate the predicate.

questions.prompt: $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\ \exists y \in \mathbb{R}:\ y^2 = x$.
questions.explanation: For $x = -1$ there is no real $y$ with $y^2 = -1$, since $y^2 \ge 0$ for every real $y$.

questions.prompt: $\exists x \in \mathbb{R}\ \forall y \in \mathbb{R}:\ xy = 0$.
questions.explanation: Take the witness $x = 0$: then $0 \cdot y = 0$ for every real $y$.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about real numbers are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Take $y = -x$, $y = x^2 + 1$ and $y = \sqrt{x}$ respectively. The second fails because one $y$ cannot satisfy $y = -x$ for every $x$ (try $x = 0$ and $x = 1$), and no real square is negative.

questions.prompt: A function $f$ is bounded above if $\exists M \in \mathbb{R}\ \forall x:\ f(x) \le M$. Which statement says that $f$ is **not** bounded above?
questions.explanation: Swap each quantifier and negate the predicate: $\forall M\ \exists x:\ f(x) > M$. The first forgets to swap the quantifiers; the second demands that every value beat every $M$; the third swaps the order and would need a single value $f(x)$ above every real number, which is impossible.

questions.prompt: In the true statement $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}\ \exists y \in \mathbb{R}:\ y > x$, the choice of $y$ may depend on…
options: nothing: a single $y$ must work for all $x$
questions.explanation: Because $\exists y$ comes after $\forall x$, $y$ is chosen once $x$ is known, e.g. $y = x + 1$. A single $y$ for all $x$ is what $\exists y\ \forall x$ would demand.

questions.prompt: The statement $\forall x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 > 0$ is true.
questions.explanation: $x = 0$ is a counterexample: $0^2 = 0$, which is not greater than $0$. With $\ge$ in place of $>$ the statement would be true.

questions.prompt: The statement $\forall n \in \mathbb{N},\ n^2 \ge 2n$ is false, with $\mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$. Which natural number $n$ is the only counterexample?
questions.explanation: For $n = 1$: $1 \ge 2$ is false. For $n \ge 2$, $n^2 = n \cdot n \ge 2n$, so the claim holds. So $n = 1$ is the only counterexample.

questions.prompt: Take $\mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$. Which of these statements are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $n = 0$ is a witness in $\mathbb{Z}$; $x = 3$ is the only solution of $2x = 6$; real squares are never negative; and $x = \sqrt{2}$ is a witness. Only the first is false: $1$ is the smallest natural number.

questions.prompt: The statement $\exists!\, x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 = 4$ is true.
questions.explanation: $\exists!$ means exactly one, but both $x = 2$ and $x = -2$ satisfy $x^2 = 4$. The statement $\exists x \in \mathbb{R},\ x^2 = 4$ (at least one) is true.

questions.prompt: What is the negation of $\forall x > 0\ \exists y > 0:\ y < x$?
questions.explanation: Swap both quantifiers, keep their order and the restrictions $x > 0$, $y > 0$, and negate $y < x$ to $y \ge x$. The first negates the restrictions, the third does not swap the quantifiers, and the fourth negates $<$ as $>$, missing $y = x$.

questions.prompt: Which is a complete proof of $\exists n \in \mathbb{Z},\ n^2 = n$?
options: Let $n$ be an arbitrary integer; then $n^2 = n$.
Take $n = 0$: it is an integer and $0^2 = 0$.
Assume $n^2 \ne n$ for every integer $n$; this is impossible for some reason.
questions.explanation: One witness proves an $\exists$ statement, and $n = 0$ works (so does $n = 1$). The first option is false: $n = 2$ gives $4 \ne 2$. The third is false as well as vague (only $0$ and $1$ work), and the fourth gives no actual reason.

concepts.title: Set theory and set operations
concepts.summary: Subsets, unions, intersections, complements, and proving two sets are equal.

blocks.title: The language of collections
blocks.md:
**In this lesson you will learn to:**
- describe sets by listing and by a property, and read the notation $\in$, $\subseteq$, $\emptyset$
- tell an element of a set apart from a subset
- form unions, intersections, differences, complements, power sets and Cartesian products
- prove two sets are equal by **double inclusion**

**You need:** lesson 1.2 (and, or, not, implies, De Morgan's laws, vacuous truth) and lesson 1.3 ($\forall$, $\exists$, and $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{R}$).

## Sets and elements

Almost every object in analysis is a set: the numbers a function accepts, the values of a sequence, an interval on the number line. Sets give one precise language for all of them.

A **set** is a collection of objects, called its **elements**. We write $x \in A$ ("$x$ is in $A$") if $x$ is an element of $A$, and $x \notin A$ if not.

Two ways to describe a set:
- **List** the elements in curly brackets: $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$.
- **Give a property**: $B = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 < 2\}$, read "the set of real $x$ **such that** $x^2 < 2$". The colon means "such that". This is **set-builder notation**.

Only membership matters. Order and repetition are ignored: $\{1, 2, 2\} = \{2, 1\}$, a set with **two** elements.

The **empty set** $\emptyset$ has no elements at all. For example, $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 = -1\} = \emptyset$.

**Standard sets.** $\mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$, $\mathbb{Z}$ (integers), $\mathbb{Q}$ (rationals: fractions $\tfrac{p}{q}$ with $p, q \in \mathbb{Z}$, $q \ne 0$) and $\mathbb{R}$ (reals).

**Intervals** are sets of reals between two numbers $a < b$. A square bracket includes the endpoint, a round one excludes it:

$$[a, b] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : a \le x \le b\}, \qquad (a, b) = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : a < x < b\}.$$

Mixed forms such as $(a, b]$ include only $b$. So $1 \in [1, 2]$ but $1 \notin (1, 2)$.

blocks.question: How many elements does $\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : -1 \le x < 3\}$ have?
blocks.explanation: The integers $x$ with $-1 \le x < 3$ are $-1, 0, 1, 2$: four elements. $-1$ is included because of $\le$; $3$ is excluded because of $<$. Infinitely many would be right for real $x$, but the set only takes integers.

blocks.md:
## Subsets

$A$ is a **subset** of $B$, written $A \subseteq B$, if every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$:

$$A \subseteq B \iff \forall x\ (x \in A \Rightarrow x \in B).$$

**Examples:**
- $\{1, 2\} \subseteq \{1, 2, 3\}$.
- $A \subseteq A$ for every set $A$: each element of $A$ is in $A$.
- $\mathbb{N} \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Q} \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, and $(0, 1) \subseteq [0, 1]$.
- **Edge case:** $\emptyset \subseteq A$ for **every** set $A$. The condition "$x \in \emptyset \Rightarrow x \in A$" has a false hypothesis for every $x$, so it is vacuously true (lesson 1.2).

**Non-example.** $\{1, 4\} \not\subseteq \{1, 2, 3\}$, because $4$ is in the first set but not the second. To show $A \not\subseteq B$, one element of $A$ outside $B$ is enough. This is the negation rule from lesson 1.3: $\neg\forall$ becomes $\exists$.

**How to prove $A \subseteq B$.** Let $x \in A$ be arbitrary, then show $x \in B$.

If $A \subseteq B$ and $A \ne B$, we call $A$ a **proper subset** and may write $A \subsetneq B$.

blocks.title: Element or subset?
blocks.md:
$\in$ relates an **element** to a set; $\subseteq$ relates a **set** to a set. For $A = \{1, 2\}$: $1 \in A$ and $\{1\} \subseteq A$, but $\{1\} \notin A$ and "$1 \subseteq A$" is meaningless.

Sets can themselves be elements. $\emptyset$ (no elements) differs from $\{\emptyset\}$, a box containing one thing, namely an empty box. Note that $\emptyset \subseteq A$ for **every** set $A$, but $\emptyset \in A$ only if $A$ actually lists $\emptyset$ as an element.

blocks.question: Let $A = \{1, \{2\}\}$. Which statement is true?
blocks.explanation: The elements of $A$ are $1$ and the set $\{2\}$, so $\{2\} \in A$. The number $2$ is not an element of $A$, which is why $\{2\} \subseteq A$ and $\{1, 2\} \subseteq A$ both fail.

blocks.md:
## Equal sets and double inclusion

The same set can be described in very different ways. For example,

$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 = 1\} = \{-1, 1\}.$$

Two sets are **equal** when they have exactly the same elements. Equivalently, each is a subset of the other. This gives the method of **double inclusion**:

$$A = B \iff (A \subseteq B \text{ and } B \subseteq A).$$

So to prove $A = B$ you prove two things: every element of $A$ is in $B$, and every element of $B$ is in $A$. Forgetting the second half is the classic mistake.

**Example.** Show $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 = 1\} = \{-1, 1\}$.
- ($\subseteq$) If $x^2 = 1$, then $x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1) = 0$, so $x = 1$ or $x = -1$.
- ($\supseteq$) $1^2 = 1$ and $(-1)^2 = 1$.

**Non-example.** $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 = 1\} = \{1\}$ is false. Here $\{1\} \subseteq \{x : x^2 = 1\}$ holds, but the other inclusion fails at $x = -1$. Checking only one direction would wrongly "prove" it.

blocks.title: Proving two sets are equal
nodes: Show $A \subseteq B$: let $x \in A$ be arbitrary and deduce $x \in B$
Show $B \subseteq A$: let $x \in B$ be arbitrary and deduce $x \in A$

blocks.md:
## Operations on sets

Just as $\land$, $\lor$ and $\neg$ build new propositions, these operations build new sets. Each one is a connective from lesson 1.2 in disguise.

- **Union** ("or"): $A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}$.
- **Intersection** ("and"): $A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}$.
- **Difference**: $A \setminus B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \notin B\}$, read "$A$ minus $B$".
- **Complement** ("not"): when all sets lie inside a fixed **universal set** $U$, $A^c = U \setminus A$.

**Examples** with $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$, $B = \{2, 3, 4\}$, $U = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$:
- $A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ (each element listed once).
- $A \cap B = \{2, 3\}$.
- $A \setminus B = \{1\}$ but $B \setminus A = \{4\}$: order matters.
- $A^c = \{4, 5\}$. The complement depends on $U$: with $U = \mathbb{N}$ it would be infinite.

**Edge cases:** if $A$ and $B$ share no elements, $A \cap B = \emptyset$ and we call them **disjoint**, e.g. $\{1, 2\} \cap \{3\} = \emptyset$. Also $A \cup \emptyset = A$ and $A \cap \emptyset = \emptyset$.

**With intervals:** $[0, 2] \cup [1, 3] = [0, 3]$, and $[0, 2] \cap (1, 3) = (1, 2]$. Check endpoints one at a time: $1$ is not in $(1, 3)$, so it is not in the intersection.

blocks.prompt: Match each set to its description, where $A, B \subseteq U$.

pairs.right: Elements in at least one of $A$, $B$
Elements of $A$ that are not in $B$
Elements of $U$ that are not in $A$

blocks.question: What is $[0, 2] \setminus (1, 3)$?
blocks.explanation: Keep the $x$ with $0 \le x \le 2$ that are **not** in $(1, 3)$, i.e. not $1 < x < 3$. That leaves $0 \le x \le 1$. The point $1$ stays, because $1 \notin (1, 3)$. $(1, 2]$ is the intersection, not the difference, and $[0, 3)$ is close to the union.

blocks.md:
## Power sets and Cartesian products

Two more ways to build sets. Both appear constantly later: the Cartesian product is how relations (lesson 1.5) and functions (lesson 1.6) are defined.

**Power set.** $\mathcal{P}(A)$ is the set of **all subsets** of $A$.
- $\mathcal{P}(\{1, 2\}) = \{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1, 2\}\}$: four elements. Do not forget $\emptyset$ and the whole set.
- If $A$ has $n$ elements, $\mathcal{P}(A)$ has $2^n$: for each element, decide "in" or "out".
- **Edge case:** $\mathcal{P}(\emptyset) = \{\emptyset\}$, which has $2^0 = 1$ element. It is not empty.

**Cartesian product.** $A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A,\ b \in B\}$, the set of **ordered pairs** with first entry from $A$ and second from $B$.
- $\{1, 2\} \times \{x, y\} = \{(1, x), (1, y), (2, x), (2, y)\}$.
- Order inside a pair matters: $(1, 2) \ne (2, 1)$, unlike the sets $\{1, 2\} = \{2, 1\}$.
- If $A$ has $m$ elements and $B$ has $n$, then $A \times B$ has $mn$.
- **Edge case:** $A \times \emptyset = \emptyset$: there is no second entry to choose.
- $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$, written $\mathbb{R}^2$, is the coordinate plane.

blocks.question: How many elements does $\mathcal{P}(\emptyset)$ have?
blocks.explanation: Every set is a subset of itself, so $\emptyset \subseteq \emptyset$ and $\mathcal{P}(\emptyset) = \{\emptyset\}$. This fits the rule $2^n$ with $n = 0$. The set $\{\emptyset\}$ has one element, so it is not empty.

cards.back:
**Every** element of $A$ is in $B$.

*Example:* $\{1, 2\} \subseteq \{1, 2, 3\}$, and $\emptyset \subseteq A$ for every $A$.

$A = B$ exactly when $A \subseteq B$ **and** $B \subseteq A$.

*Example:* $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x^2 = 1\} = \{-1, 1\}$, checked both ways.

Elements of $A$ that are **not** in $B$. Order matters.

*Example:* $\{1, 2, 3\} \setminus \{2, 3, 4\} = \{1\}$.

$U \setminus A$: everything in the **universal set** $U$ that is not in $A$.

*Example:* $U = \{1, \dots, 5\}$, $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$: $A^c = \{4, 5\}$.

The set of **all subsets** of $A$; $2^n$ of them if $A$ has $n$ elements.

*Example:* $\mathcal{P}(\{1, 2\}) = \{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1, 2\}\}$.

All **ordered pairs** $(a, b)$ with $a \in A$, $b \in B$.

*Example:* $\{1, 2\} \times \{0\} = \{(1, 0), (2, 0)\}$.

Sets with **no element in common**: $A \cap B = \emptyset$.

*Example:* the even and the odd integers.

blocks.question: You want to prove that two sets $A$ and $B$ are equal. You have shown that every element of $A$ lies in $B$. What is still missing?
options: Show that every element of $B$ lies in $A$
blocks.explanation: Double inclusion needs $A \subseteq B$ **and** $B \subseteq A$. With only one direction, $B$ could be bigger: $\{1\} \subseteq \{1, 2\}$ but they are not equal. Disjointness would contradict equality (unless both are empty), and checking examples is not a proof.

blocks.title: De Morgan's law for sets: $(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c$

steps.title: Plan: double inclusion
steps.md: Let $A, B \subseteq U$. We show each side is a subset of the other. In words, the claim is "not in either" equals "not in $A$ and not in $B$".

steps.title: Show $(A \cup B)^c \subseteq A^c \cap B^c$
steps.md:
Let $x \in (A \cup B)^c$ be arbitrary. Then $x \in U$ and $x 
otin A \cup B$. If $x$ were in $A$, it would be in $A \cup B$; so $x 
otin A$, that is, $x \in A^c$. In the same way $x 
otin B$, so $x \in B^c$. Hence $x \in A^c \cap B^c$.

steps.title: Show $A^c \cap B^c \subseteq (A \cup B)^c$
steps.md:
Let $x \in A^c \cap B^c$ be arbitrary. Then $x \in U$, $x 
otin A$ and $x 
otin B$. So $x$ is in neither set, which means $x 
otin A \cup B$; that is, $x \in (A \cup B)^c$.

We start again with a **new** arbitrary $x$: the first half tells us nothing about elements of $A^c \cap B^c$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.md:
Each side is a subset of the other, so $(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c$. $ lacksquare$

The logic underneath is De Morgan for propositions (lesson 1.2): $
eg(x \in A \lor x \in B) \equiv (x 
otin A) \land (x 
otin B)$.

blocks.question: In the proof above, why does each half begin "let $x$ be **arbitrary**" rather than with a specific element such as $x = 1$?
options: Because a subset claim is a "for all" statement, so the argument must work for every element
Because arbitrary elements make the algebra easier
blocks.explanation: $A \subseteq B$ means $\forall x\ (x \in A \Rightarrow x \in B)$. As in lesson 1.3, a "for all" claim is proved with an arbitrary element; one specific element would only check one case. Whether $1 \in U$ is beside the point, and there is no algebra here.

blocks.prompt: Put these steps in order to prove $A \setminus B \subseteq A \cap B^c$, where $A, B \subseteq U$.
items: By the definition of difference, $x \in A$ and $x \notin B$.
Since $x \in A \subseteq U$ and $x \notin B$, we have $x \in B^c$.
So $x \in A$ and $x \in B^c$, that is, $x \in A \cap B^c$. Hence $A \setminus B \subseteq A \cap B^c$.

blocks.title: Your turn: a distributive law
blocks.problem: Prove that $A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$ for all sets $A$, $B$, $C$. Use double inclusion, and split into cases where an "or" appears.
blocks.solution:
**($\subseteq$)** Let $x \in A \cap (B \cup C)$. Then $x \in A$, and $x \in B$ or $x \in C$.
- If $x \in B$: $x \in A$ and $x \in B$, so $x \in A \cap B$.
- If $x \in C$: $x \in A$ and $x \in C$, so $x \in A \cap C$.

In either case $x \in (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$.

**($\supseteq$)** Let $x \in (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$. Then $x \in A \cap B$ or $x \in A \cap C$.
- If $x \in A \cap B$: $x \in A$ and $x \in B \subseteq B \cup C$.
- If $x \in A \cap C$: $x \in A$ and $x \in C \subseteq B \cup C$.

In either case $x \in A$ and $x \in B \cup C$, so $x \in A \cap (B \cup C)$.

By double inclusion the sets are equal. $\blacksquare$

**Check your version:** did you prove **both** inclusions? Did you start each with an arbitrary element? Did every "or" lead to a case split covering both possibilities?

items.q: Is $\{1, 2, 2\}$ a set with three elements?
items.a: No. A set only records **whether** something is a member, so $\{1, 2, 2\} = \{1, 2\}$ has two elements. Listing an element twice changes nothing.

items.q: Why is the empty set a subset of everything? It feels like it should be a subset of nothing.
items.a: To fail to be a subset of $A$, $\emptyset$ would need an element outside $A$. It has no elements at all, so it can never fail. Formally, "$x \in \emptyset \Rightarrow x \in A$" is vacuously true.

items.q: Can a Venn diagram prove a set identity?
items.a: A Venn diagram is a good way to **guess** an identity or spot a counterexample, but it shows one picture of the sets. A proof uses an arbitrary element and double inclusion.

items.q: What universal set should I use for a complement?
items.a: Whatever the problem fixes, often $\mathbb{R}$ in analysis. The complement changes with $U$: the complement of $\{1, 2\}$ in $\{1, 2, 3\}$ is $\{3\}$, but in $\mathbb{N}$ it is $\{3, 4, 5, \dots\}$.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.md:
- $x \in A$ says $x$ is an element; $A \subseteq B$ says every element of $A$ is in $B$. $\emptyset \subseteq A$ for every $A$.
- Order and repetition do not matter in a set; they do matter in an ordered pair.
- $\cup$, $\cap$ and complement mirror "or", "and" and "not"; $A \setminus B$ keeps what is in $A$ but not $B$.
- $\mathcal{P}(A)$ has $2^n$ elements when $A$ has $n$; $A \times B$ has $mn$ when $A$, $B$ have $m$, $n$.
- To prove $A = B$, show $A \subseteq B$ **and** $B \subseteq A$, each with an arbitrary element.

questions.prompt: Let $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $B = \{2, 3, 4\}$. What is $A \setminus B$?
questions.explanation: $A \setminus B$ keeps the elements of $A$ not in $B$: only $1$. $\{4\}$ is $B \setminus A$, $\{2, 3\}$ is $A \cap B$, and $\{1, 4\}$ contains $4$, which is not in $A$.

questions.prompt: How many elements does the power set of $\{a, b, c, d\}$ have?
questions.explanation: A set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets: each element is either in or out. Here $2^4 = 16$.

questions.prompt: $\emptyset \subseteq A$ for every set $A$.
questions.explanation: The condition "$x \in \emptyset \Rightarrow x \in A$" has a false hypothesis for every $x$, so it is vacuously true.

questions.prompt: $A \setminus B = B \setminus A$ for all sets $A$ and $B$.
questions.explanation: With $A = \{1\}$ and $B = \emptyset$: $A \setminus B = \{1\}$ but $B \setminus A = \emptyset$.

questions.prompt: Which identities hold for **all** sets $A, B, C$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The two distributive laws hold, and anything in both sets is in at least one. The third is wrong: the correct law is $A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C)$. Counterexample: $A = B = \{1\}$, $C = \emptyset$ gives $\emptyset$ on the left and $\{1\}$ on the right.
We need $0 \le x \le 2$ and $1 < x < 3$, i.e. $1 < x \le 2$. The point $1$ is excluded because $1 \notin (1, 3)$; the point $2$ is included because it lies in both. $[0, 3)$ is the union.

questions.prompt: If $A$ has $3$ elements and $B$ has $4$ elements, how many elements does $A \times B$ have?
questions.explanation: An ordered pair $(a, b)$ is a choice of one of $3$ values of $a$ and one of $4$ values of $b$: $3 \cdot 4 = 12$. Adding gives $7$, which would count elements of a union of disjoint sets, not pairs.
Two sets are equal when they have the same elements. Both sets contain exactly $1$ and $2$; repetition is ignored.

questions.prompt: $\emptyset = \{\emptyset\}$.
questions.explanation: $\emptyset$ has no elements, while $\{\emptyset\}$ has one element, namely $\emptyset$. Sets with different elements are different.

questions.prompt: How many elements does the set $\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x^2 < 5\}$ have?
questions.explanation: The integers with $x^2 < 5$ are $-2, -1, 0, 1, 2$ (since $2^2 = 4 < 5$ but $3^2 = 9$). Remember the negative integers and $0$.

questions.prompt: Let $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $1$ is an element of $A$, and both $1$ and $3$ are in $A$, so $\{1, 3\} \subseteq A$. The elements of $A$ are numbers, so neither the set $\{1\}$ nor $\emptyset$ is an element (though both are subsets). $\{4\} \not\subseteq A$ because $4 \notin A$.
$A^c = U \setminus A$: the elements of $U$ not in $A$, which are $1, 3, 5$. The complement stays inside $U$, so $7, 9, \dots$ are not included.

concepts.title: Relations and equivalence relations
concepts.summary: Reflexive, symmetric, transitive: how "sameness" splits a set into classes.

blocks.title: Making "the same in some respect" precise
blocks.md:
**In this lesson you will learn to:**
- describe a relation as a set of ordered pairs
- test a relation for the reflexive, symmetric, transitive and antisymmetric properties
- recognise an equivalence relation and find its equivalence classes
- see why equivalence classes split a set into non-overlapping pieces

**You need:** lesson 1.4 (sets, subsets, ordered pairs and $A \times B$), and $\forall$ and $\Rightarrow$ from lessons 1.2–1.3.

## Relations

Mathematics often compares two objects: $2 < 5$, "$3$ divides $12$", "$7$ and $1$ are both odd". A **relation** captures any such comparison in one format.

A **relation** on a set $A$ is a subset $R \subseteq A \times A$. Recall from lesson 1.4 that $A \times A$ is the set of ordered pairs $(a, b)$ with $a, b \in A$. We write $a \mathrel{R} b$, "$a$ is related to $b$", when $(a, b) \in R$.

**Examples:**
- "Less than" on $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ is the set $\{(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)\}$. The pair $(2, 1)$ is not in it, because $2 < 1$ is false. Order in the pair matters.
- Equality on $\mathbb{R}$: $x \mathrel{R} y$ when $x = y$.

**Divisibility.** For integers $m$ and $n$, "$m$ **divides** $n$", written $m \mid n$, means $n = mk$ for some integer $k$.
- $3 \mid 12$, because $12 = 3 \cdot 4$.
- $3 \mid 0$, because $0 = 3 \cdot 0$. Every integer divides $0$.
- **Non-example:** $3 \nmid 7$: no integer $k$ gives $7 = 3k$.

Do not confuse $3 \mid 12$ (a statement, true or false) with $\tfrac{12}{3}$ (a number, $4$). Also $3 \mid 12$ is true while $12 \mid 3$ is false.

blocks.question: Let $R$ be the relation "$a \mid b$" on $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$. Which pair is **not** in $R$?
blocks.explanation: $(4, 2) \in R$ would mean $4 \mid 2$, i.e. $2 = 4k$ for an integer $k$. That needs $k = \tfrac12$, so it fails. $1 \mid 3$ ($3 = 1 \cdot 3$), $2 \mid 4$ ($4 = 2 \cdot 2$) and $3 \mid 3$ ($3 = 3 \cdot 1$) all hold.

blocks.md:
## Reflexive and symmetric

Not every relation behaves like "sameness". These properties pick out the ones that do.

**Reflexive:** every element is related to itself.

$$\forall a \in A:\ a \mathrel{R} a.$$

- $=$ and $\le$ on $\mathbb{R}$ are reflexive: $x = x$ and $x \le x$.
- $<$ is **not**: $1 < 1$ is false. One failure is enough.
- **Edge case:** on $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$, the relation $\{(1, 1), (2, 2)\}$ is **not** reflexive, because $(3, 3)$ is missing. Reflexive means **every** element, not just some.

**Symmetric:** whenever $a$ is related to $b$, $b$ is related to $a$.

$$\forall a, b \in A:\ a \mathrel{R} b \Rightarrow b \mathrel{R} a.$$

- "$a - b$ is even" on $\mathbb{Z}$ is symmetric: if $a - b = 2k$, then $b - a = 2(-k)$.
- $\le$ is **not**: $1 \le 2$ but $2 \not\le 1$.
- **Edge case:** the empty relation $R = \emptyset$ is symmetric. The hypothesis $a \mathrel{R} b$ never holds, so the implication is vacuously true (lesson 1.2).

To **disprove** either property, give one specific counterexample, as with any "for all" statement (lesson 1.3).

blocks.question: On $\mathbb{Z}$, define $a \mathrel{R} b$ when $a + b$ is even. Which describes $R$?
blocks.explanation: Reflexive: $a + a = 2a$ is even for every integer $a$. Symmetric: $a + b = b + a$, so if one is even so is the other. Students often test only a few values and miss that $2a$ is **always** even, including for negative $a$ and $a = 0$.

blocks.md:
## Transitive and antisymmetric

**Transitive:** relations can be chained.

$$\forall a, b, c \in A:\ (a \mathrel{R} b \land b \mathrel{R} c) \Rightarrow a \mathrel{R} c.$$

- $<$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is transitive: $a < b$ and $b < c$ give $a < c$.
- $\mid$ is transitive: if $b = ak$ and $c = bl$, then $c = a(kl)$.
- **Non-example:** "$|x - y| < 1$" on $\mathbb{R}$ (the numbers are less than $1$ apart). $0$ and $0.6$ are related, $0.6$ and $1.2$ are related, but $0$ and $1.2$ are not. Being close is not transitive.

**Antisymmetric:** two different elements are never related both ways.

$$\forall a, b \in A:\ (a \mathrel{R} b \land b \mathrel{R} a) \Rightarrow a = b.$$

- $\le$ is antisymmetric: $a \le b$ and $b \le a$ force $a = b$.
- $\mid$ on the **positive** integers is antisymmetric. On all of $\mathbb{Z}$ it is not: $2 \mid -2$ and $-2 \mid 2$ but $2 \ne -2$.

**Edge case:** antisymmetric does **not** mean "not symmetric". Equality $=$ is both symmetric and antisymmetric. Relations that are reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, like $\le$, are called **partial orders**. They describe ranking, not sameness.

blocks.prompt: Match each relation on $\mathbb{R}$ to its properties.

pairs.right: Transitive, but neither reflexive nor symmetric

blocks.title: Symmetric and transitive does not give reflexive
blocks.md: A tempting "proof": if $a \sim b$ then $b \sim a$ by symmetry, so $a \sim a$ by transitivity. The flaw is that it assumes **some** $b$ with $a \sim b$ exists. On $A = \{1, 2\}$ the relation $R = \{(1, 1)\}$ is symmetric and transitive, but not reflexive because $(2, 2) \notin R$. Nothing is related to $2$, so the argument never gets started.

## Equivalence relations and classes

An **equivalence relation** is a relation that is **reflexive, symmetric and transitive**. These are exactly the properties of "is the same as", so equivalence relations make precise the idea of two objects being the same **in some respect**. We usually write $a \sim b$, read "$a$ is equivalent to $b$".

The **equivalence class** of $a$ is the set of everything equivalent to $a$:

$$[a] = \{x \in A : x \sim a\}.$$

**Example: same parity.** On $\mathbb{Z}$, let $a \sim b$ when $a - b$ is even. It is reflexive ($a - a = 0$ is even), symmetric (shown above) and transitive (if $a - b = 2k$ and $b - c = 2l$, then $a - c = 2(k + l)$). Its classes:

$$[0] = \{\dots, -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, \dots\}, \qquad [1] = \{\dots, -3, -1, 1, 3, \dots\}.$$

**Edge case:** $[2] = [0]$ and $[-5] = [1]$. A class has many names, one for each of its elements. There are only **two** classes, not infinitely many.

**Example: equality.** For $=$ on $\mathbb{R}$, $[x] = \{x\}$: each class has one element.

**Non-example:** $\le$ is not an equivalence relation (not symmetric), so it has no equivalence classes.

blocks.question: For the parity relation on $\mathbb{Z}$ ($a \sim b$ when $a - b$ is even), which set is $[-3]$?
blocks.explanation: $x \in [-3]$ when $x - (-3) = x + 3$ is even, which happens exactly when $x$ is odd. So $[-3] = [1]$ is the set of odd integers. The fourth option is the multiples of $3$, which belongs to a different relation.

blocks.md:
## Classes form a partition

In every example so far, the classes split the set into pieces that do not overlap. This always happens.

A **partition** of $A$ is a collection of **nonempty** subsets of $A$ that are **pairwise disjoint** (any two different pieces share no element) and whose **union** is $A$. Think of cutting a cake: every crumb is in exactly one piece.

**Theorem.** If $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $A$, then for all $a, b \in A$ either $[a] = [b]$ or $[a] \cap [b] = \emptyset$, and every element of $A$ lies in some class. So the equivalence classes form a partition of $A$.

**Example: congruence modulo $m$.** Fix an integer $m \ge 2$. On $\mathbb{Z}$, define

$$a \equiv b \pmod m \iff m \mid (a - b),$$

read "$a$ is congruent to $b$ modulo $m$". It means $a$ and $b$ leave the same remainder on division by $m$. For $m = 3$ there are three classes:

$$[0] = \{\dots, -3, 0, 3, \dots\}, \quad [1] = \{\dots, -2, 1, 4, \dots\}, \quad [2] = \{\dots, -1, 2, 5, \dots\}.$$

Note $-1 \in [2]$, since $-1 - 2 = -3$. Negative numbers trip people up. Parity is the case $m = 2$.

**Non-example of a partition:** $\{\{1, 2\}, \{2, 3\}\}$ is not a partition of $\{1, 2, 3\}$, because $2$ lies in two pieces. Classes of an equivalence relation can never overlap like this.

blocks.question: Which of these is a partition of $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$?
blocks.explanation: $\{1\}$ and $\{2, 3, 4\}$ are nonempty, disjoint and together cover $A$. The first misses $4$; the second puts $2$ in two pieces; the fourth includes the empty set, and the pieces of a partition must be nonempty.

cards.back:
A **subset** $R$ of $A \times A$; write $a \mathrel{R} b$ when $(a, b) \in R$.

*Example:* $<$ on $\{1, 2, 3\}$ is $\{(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)\}$.

**Every** element is related to itself: $a \mathrel{R} a$ for all $a$.

*Example:* $\le$ is reflexive; $<$ is not.

$a \mathrel{R} b$ **implies** $b \mathrel{R} a$.

*Example:* "$a - b$ is even" is symmetric; $\le$ is not.

$a \mathrel{R} b$ and $b \mathrel{R} c$ **imply** $a \mathrel{R} c$.

*Example:* $<$ is transitive; "$|x - y| < 1$" is not.

A relation that is **reflexive, symmetric and transitive**.

*Example:* congruence modulo $3$ on $\mathbb{Z}$.

$\{x \in A : x \sim a\}$, **everything equivalent** to $a$.

*Example:* for parity on $\mathbb{Z}$, $[1]$ is the odd integers, and $[1] = [5]$.

**Nonempty**, pairwise **disjoint** subsets of $A$ whose union is $A$.

*Example:* $\{\{1\}, \{2, 3\}\}$ partitions $\{1, 2, 3\}$.

"$m$ **divides** $n$": $n = mk$ for some integer $k$. A statement, not a number.

*Example:* $3 \mid 12$ and $3 \mid 0$, but $3 \nmid 7$.

blocks.question: On the set of all students in a school, "$a \sim b$ when $a$ and $b$ have the same birthday month". What are its equivalence classes?
options: One class for each month in which at least one student was born
It is not an equivalence relation, so there are no classes
blocks.explanation: "Same birthday month" is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation. Each class is the set of students born in one particular month. A month with no students gives no class, because classes are never empty. It would be one class per student only if every student had a different month.

blocks.title: Why two classes are equal or disjoint

steps.title: Set up
steps.md: Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $A$ and $a, b \in A$. Suppose $[a] \cap [b] \neq \emptyset$. We show $[a] = [b]$. (So if two classes share anything, they are identical.)

steps.title: Pick a common element and link $a$ to $b$
steps.md:
Choose $c \in [a] \cap [b]$. Then $c \sim a$ and $c \sim b$. By symmetry $a \sim c$, and by transitivity ($a \sim c$, $c \sim b$) we get $a \sim b$.

We need symmetry first because transitivity chains $a \sim c$ with $c \sim b$, and we were given $c \sim a$, which points the wrong way.

steps.title: Show $[a] \subseteq [b]$
steps.md: Let $x \in [a]$, so $x \sim a$. With $a \sim b$, transitivity gives $x \sim b$, so $x \in [b]$.

steps.title: Show $[b] \subseteq [a]$
steps.md: By symmetry $b \sim a$. If $x \in [b]$ then $x \sim b$ and $b \sim a$, so $x \sim a$ and $x \in [a]$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.md: By double inclusion (lesson 1.4) $[a] = [b]$. Also each $a$ lies in its own class, since $a \sim a$ by reflexivity, so no class is empty and the classes cover $A$. $\blacksquare$

blocks.question: In the proof above, where is **reflexivity** used?
options: To show every element lies in its own class, so classes are nonempty and cover $A$
blocks.explanation: Reflexivity gives $a \sim a$, so $a \in [a]$. Without it, an element could belong to no class (as with $2$ under $R = \{(1, 1)\}$ on $\{1, 2\}$). Turning $c \sim a$ round uses symmetry, and chaining uses transitivity.

blocks.prompt: Put these steps in order to prove that "$a \sim b$ when $5 \mid (a - b)$" is **transitive** on $\mathbb{Z}$.
items: Let $a, b, c \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $a \sim b$ and $b \sim c$.
Then $a - b = 5k$ and $b - c = 5l$ for some integers $k$ and $l$.
Since $k + l$ is an integer, $5 \mid (a - c)$, so $a \sim c$.

blocks.title: Your turn: congruence modulo 3
blocks.problem: Prove that $a \sim b \iff 3 \mid (a - b)$ is an equivalence relation on $\mathbb{Z}$, and describe its equivalence classes. Check the three properties one at a time, each with arbitrary integers.
blocks.solution:
**Reflexive.** For any $a \in \mathbb{Z}$, $a - a = 0 = 3 \cdot 0$, so $3 \mid (a - a)$ and $a \sim a$.

**Symmetric.** If $a \sim b$, then $a - b = 3k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. So $b - a = 3(-k)$ with $-k \in \mathbb{Z}$, and $b \sim a$.

**Transitive.** If $a \sim b$ and $b \sim c$, then $a - b = 3k$ and $b - c = 3l$ for some integers $k, l$. Adding, $a - c = 3(k + l)$, so $a \sim c$.

Hence $\sim$ is an equivalence relation.

**Classes.** Every integer can be written as $a = 3q + s$ with $q \in \mathbb{Z}$ and remainder $s \in \{0, 1, 2\}$, and then $a - s = 3q$, so $a \sim s$. Different $s, s' \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ are not equivalent, since $s - s'$ is $\pm 1$ or $\pm 2$, not a multiple of $3$. So there are exactly three classes:

$$[0] = \{\dots, -3, 0, 3, 6, \dots\}, \quad [1] = \{\dots, -2, 1, 4, 7, \dots\}, \quad [2] = \{\dots, -1, 2, 5, 8, \dots\}. \ \blacksquare$$

**Check your version:** did you use different letters $k$ and $l$ in the transitive step? Did you say why $-k$ and $k + l$ are integers? Did you show the three classes are different, not just list them?

items.q: Is a relation just a rule, like "$<$"?
items.a: Formally it is a set of ordered pairs, which avoids any vagueness about what the rule means. In practice we describe it by a rule and then use the set whenever precision matters. On a small set you can list the pairs: "$<$" on $\{1, 2, 3\}$ is $\{(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)\}$.

items.q: Do all equivalence classes have the same size?
items.a: No. On $\{1, 2, 3\}$, the equivalence relation $\{(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2), (2,1)\}$ has classes $\{1, 2\}$ and $\{3\}$. They are never empty and never overlap, but their sizes can differ.

items.q: If I check reflexive, symmetric and transitive on a few examples, is that enough?
items.a: No. Each property is a "for all" statement (lesson 1.3), so you need an argument with arbitrary elements. A few examples can only **disprove** a property, by giving a counterexample.

items.q: Why does analysis care about equivalence relations?
items.a: Many constructions glue objects together. For instance, the fractions $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac24$ are the same rational number: rationals are classes of pairs $(p, q)$ under "$pq' = p'q$". Lesson 2.1 looks at $\mathbb{Q}$ more closely.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.md:
- A **relation** on $A$ is a subset of $A \times A$; $a \mathrel{R} b$ means $(a, b) \in R$.
- **Reflexive**: every $a \mathrel{R} a$. **Symmetric**: $a \mathrel{R} b \Rightarrow b \mathrel{R} a$. **Transitive**: $a \mathrel{R} b$, $b \mathrel{R} c \Rightarrow a \mathrel{R} c$. Disprove each with one counterexample.
- An **equivalence relation** has all three; $\le$ (reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive) is a partial order instead.
- The class $[a]$ is everything equivalent to $a$; different names can give the same class, such as $[0] = [2]$ for parity.
- Equivalence classes are equal or disjoint and cover $A$: they form a **partition**.

questions.prompt: On $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$, the relation $R = \{(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2), (2,1)\}$ is an equivalence relation. How many equivalence classes does it have?
questions.explanation: The classes are $[1] = [2] = \{1, 2\}$ and $[3] = \{3\}$: two classes. $[1]$ and $[2]$ are two names for the same class.

questions.prompt: Every relation on a nonempty set that is symmetric and transitive is also reflexive.
questions.explanation: On $\{1, 2\}$, $R = \{(1, 1)\}$ is symmetric and transitive but $(2, 2) \notin R$. The "proof" via symmetry and transitivity needs an element related to $2$, which does not exist.

questions.prompt: Which of these are equivalence relations? Select all that apply.
options: On $\mathbb{Z}$: $a \sim b$ iff $a - b$ is even
On the set of lines in the plane: $\ell \sim m$ iff $\ell$ and $m$ are parallel or equal

questions.prompt: For congruence modulo $5$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, which set is $[7]$?
questions.explanation: $[7]$ contains all integers $x$ with $5 \mid (x - 7)$, i.e. $x = 7 + 5k$ for $k \in \mathbb{Z}$: the integers leaving remainder $2$ on division by $5$. The class is not just $\{7\}$, and it is not the multiples of $5$ or of $7$.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the equivalence classes of an equivalence relation on $A$ is correct?
options: They always all have the same size.
Any two of them have at least one element in common.
Any two are either equal or disjoint, and their union is $A$.
questions.explanation: The classes partition $A$. Each class $[a]$ contains $a$, so none is empty, but sizes may differ (as with $\{1, 2\}$ and $\{3\}$ in an earlier question).

questions.prompt: On the positive integers, the relation "$a$ divides $b$" is antisymmetric.
questions.explanation: If $a \mid b$ and $b \mid a$ with $a, b > 0$, then $a \le b$ and $b \le a$, so $a = b$. (On all of $\mathbb{Z}$ it fails: $2 \mid -2$ and $-2 \mid 2$.)

questions.prompt: The relation $<$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is reflexive.
questions.explanation: Reflexive needs $a < a$ for every $a$, but $1 < 1$ is false (in fact $a < a$ is false for every $a$). $\le$ is reflexive; $<$ is not.

questions.prompt: How many equivalence classes does congruence modulo $4$ have on $\mathbb{Z}$?
questions.explanation: Every integer leaves one of the remainders $0, 1, 2, 3$ on division by $4$, giving the classes $[0], [1], [2], [3]$. No two of these are congruent.

questions.prompt: Which properties does the relation $=$ on $\mathbb{R}$ have? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $x = x$; $x = y$ gives $y = x$; $x = y$ and $y = z$ give $x = z$; and $x = y$ and $y = x$ certainly give $x = y$. Equality shows that symmetric and antisymmetric are not opposites.

questions.prompt: On $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$, the relation $\{(1, 1), (2, 2)\}$ is reflexive.
questions.explanation: Reflexive needs $(a, a)$ for **every** $a \in A$. The pair $(3, 3)$ is missing.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a partition of $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$?
questions.explanation: The odd and even elements are nonempty, disjoint and cover the set. The second puts $5$ in two pieces, the third misses $5$, and the fourth contains the empty set, which a partition may not.
